Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe ruin of Judah under the emblem of a sharp sword.1–17The approach of the king of Babylon described.18–27The destruction of the Ammonites.28–32
The sword of judgment approaches Judah (verses 1–17)

This passage explains the parable at the end of the previous chapter.

The Lord announced that Jerusalem and the whole land would be cut down.

Everyone would learn that the judgment came from his decree against a wicked and rebellious people.

Those who proclaim God's dreadful judgment on sinners should make it clear that they do not delight in the day of suffering.

Christ's example teaches us to weep over the people whose destruction we must announce.

Whatever instruments the Lord chooses to execute judgment, he gives them the strength required for their appointed task.

The sword flashes with terror before those against whom it is drawn.

To some it is a sword; to the Lord's people it is a rod of discipline.

God is serious about this sentence, and the prophet must show the same seriousness in proclaiming it.

Nebuchadnezzar is directed toward Jerusalem (verses 18–27)

Through the Spirit of prophecy, Ezekiel foresaw Nebuchadnezzar marching from Babylon.

The king would decide his direction by divination.

Yet the Lord's wise purposes governed the outcome.

God would overthrow Judah's government until the arrival of the One whose right it is to rule.

Henry sees this as pointing beyond the immediate events to the continuing upheavals of the Jewish nation and the changes of earthly states and kingdoms.

These would prepare the way for the Messiah's kingdom throughout the earth.

The Lord secretly directs events toward his wise designs.

Even amid the most terrifying warnings of judgment, we hear a word of mercy, pointing toward the One through whom mercy comes to sinful people.

Ammon's false confidence ends in destruction (verses 28–32)

The Ammonites' diviners falsely promised victory.

The nation would ultimately lose its power and disappear from memory.

Let us be thankful that God has appointed us to serve as instruments of mercy.

We should use our understanding and abilities to do good, and keep away from those whose only skill is causing destruction.

Jerusalem is accused of many sins (verses 1–16)

The prophet was told to judge the city of bloodshed.

Jerusalem deserved that name because of its crimes.

The charges were exceedingly serious: murder, idolatry, dishonoring parents, oppression, extortion, profaning the Sabbath and holy things, sexual immorality and adultery.

At the root of these wrongs lay forgetfulness of God.

Sinners provoke him because they refuse to remember him.

Jerusalem had filled the measure of her sins.

People who surrender themselves to the rule of their sinful desires may justly be handed over to their consequences.

Those determined to be their own masters cannot expect more happiness than they can supply for themselves.

It will be a miserable portion.

Israel is like worthless dross (verses 17–22)

Among surrounding nations, Israel had once been as gold and silver compared with inferior metals.

But now the people resembled the worthless residue separated from silver in the furnace.

In God's sight, persistent sinners—especially people who profess faith but turn back to sin—are without the usefulness they were meant to have.

When the Lord brings his own people into a furnace of affliction, he watches over them like a refiner guarding his precious gold.

He keeps them there no longer than necessary.

The worthless residue is separated and the good metal made pure.

If we experience severe pain or long illness and find even these temporary trials almost unbearable, we should be warned to flee the far greater wrath to come.

Unless the Holy Spirit uses our suffering to cleanse our hearts and conduct, much worse misery may await us.

Every level of society is corrupt (verses 23–31)

People of every rank and occupation contributed to the nation's guilt.

Those who possessed authority abused it.

Even buyers and sellers found ways to oppress one another.

It is a fearful sign when judgment is beginning and the spirit of prayer has weakened.

Let everyone who fears God unite to uphold his truth and righteousness, while wicked people from every profession and class unite to oppose them.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A history of the apostacy of God's people from him, and the aggravation thereof.

Aholah and Aholibah picture Israel and Judah

The parable gives Samaria and the northern kingdom of Israel the name Aholah, meaning “her own tabernacle.”

Their places of worship came from their own inventions rather than God's command.

Jerusalem and Judah are called Aholibah, meaning “my tabernacle is in her.”

Their temple was the place God himself had chosen for his name to dwell.

The imagery and language of this passage belong to the times and circumstances in which they were used.

These humbling descriptions of fallen human nature should keep us in a spirit of repentance and sorrow over sin.

They should remove pride from our hearts and turn us away from self-righteousness.

They should also lead us to seek God's grace continually, praying that his Holy Spirit would enable us to put sinful conduct to death and live in holiness and godliness.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.23.1]
Chapter 23
A history of the apostacy of God's people from him, and the aggravation thereof.
In this parable, Samaria and Israel bear the name Aholah, "her own tabernacle;" because the places of worship those kingdoms had, were of their own devising. Jerusalem and Judah bear the name of Aholibah, "my tabernacle is in her," because their temple was the place which God himself had chosen, to put his name there. The language and figures are according to those times. Will not such humbling representations of nature keep open perpetual repentance and sorrow in the soul, hiding pride from our eyes, and taking us from self-righteousness? Will it not also prompt the soul to look to God continually for grace, that by his Holy Spirit we may mortify the deeds of the body, and live in holy conversation and godliness?

Jerusalem is pictured as a pot on the fire (verses 1–14)

The pot heated over the fire represented Jerusalem being besieged by the Chaldeans.

People of every position and class were inside the city walls and were about to become their enemies' prey.

They should have removed their sins as scum is skimmed from boiling food.

Instead, they became more corrupt, and their suffering grew worse.

Jerusalem would be leveled to the ground.

The appointed hour of judgment may appear to approach slowly, but it will certainly arrive.

How sorrowful to consider how many people gain nothing from God's appointed worship or the events of his Providence!

Ezekiel's bereavement is a sign (verses 15–27)

Mourning those who die is normally a duty.

But religion and sound judgment must restrain our grief.

We should not grieve as people without hope.

Believers need not imitate the words or gestures of those who do not know God.

The people asked Ezekiel what his strange actions meant.

The Lord was about to remove from them everything they held most precious.

Just as Ezekiel did not publicly mourn his own loss in the customary manner, the people's coming sorrow would exceed ordinary expressions of lament.

Blessed be God: we need not sink under suffering forever.

Even if every earthly comfort fails and all sorrows arrive together, a broken heart and a mourner's sincere prayer remain acceptable to him.

The Ammonites are judged for rejoicing in Judah's ruin (verses 1–7)

It is wicked to rejoice when anyone suffers, especially when the sufferers belong to God's people.

God will certainly call such cruelty to account.

Even while he permits Israel to be held captive in Babylon, he will show that he remains the God of Israel.

It is better to know the Lord while poor than to be wealthy and ignorant of him.

Moab, Edom and Philistia face judgment (verses 8–17)

The same outward event may happen to both righteous and wicked people, yet its meaning and final consequence may be entirely different.

Those who boast in any protection apart from God's power, Providence and promises will eventually be ashamed of their confidence.

People who refuse to leave vengeance in God's hands may expect his judgment to fall upon them.

The Lord's judgments are fair.

Sometimes he avenges an injury through the people who suffered it, and the justice of his action remains visible.

Those who nurture old hatreds, waiting for a chance to act upon them, are storing up wrath for the day of wrath.

God will make it appear that he is the God of Israel, though he suffers them for a time to be captives in Babylon. It is better to know Him, and to be poor, than to be rich and ignorant of him.
[Ezek.25.8-Ezek.25.17]

Those who treasure up old hatred, and watch for the opportunity of manifesting it, are treasuring up for themselves wrath against the day of wrath.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A prophecy against Tyre.

Tyre's selfish prosperity will be destroyed (verses 1–14)

It is an easily overlooked but serious sin to be secretly pleased when others decline or die because we expect to benefit, or when their downfall allows us to become more prosperous.

Such pleasure comes from selfishness and greed and from regarding the world as our source of happiness. Love for God expressly forbids that attitude.

God often brings to nothing the projects of those who hope to advance themselves through other people's ruin.

Many of the principles most commonly accepted in the world of trade directly oppose God's law.

The Lord will confront merchants whose love of money and selfishness have hardened their hearts, as they had hardened the hearts of the people of Tyre.

People have little reason to boast about goods that provoke others' envy and greed and constantly pass from one owner to another.

In acquiring, protecting and spending such wealth, people may offend God, whose anger can turn a joyful city into a heap of ruins.

The fall of Tyre warns prosperous people (verses 15–21)

Consider how important and impressive Tyre once was—and how low it would be brought.

The downfall of others should awaken us from careless confidence.

Every clear fulfillment of a biblical prophecy is like a miracle that strengthens our faith.

Everything merely earthly is vanity and frustration.

Even those whose prosperity seems most secure will soon disappear from sight and be forgotten.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.26.1-Ezek.26.14]
Chapter 26
A prophecy against Tyre.
Verses 1-14 To be secretly pleased with the death or decay of others, when we are likely to get by it; or with their fall, when we may thrive upon it, is a sin that easily besets us, yet is not thought so bad as really it is. But it comes from a selfish, covetous principle, and from that love of the world as our happiness, which the love of God expressly forbids. He often blasts the projects of those who would raise themselves on the ruin of others. The maxims most current in the trading world, are directly opposed to the law of God. But he will show himself against the money-loving, selfish traders, whose hearts, like those of Tyre, are hardened by the love of riches. Men have little cause to glory in things which stir up the envy and rapacity of others, and which are continually shifting from one to another; and in getting, keeping, and spending which, men provoke that God whose wrath turns joyous cities into ruinous heaps.
[Ezek.26.15-Ezek.26.21]
Verses 15-21 See how high, how great Tyre had been. See how low Tyre is made. The fall of others should awaken us out of security. Every discovery of the fulfilment of a Scripture prophecy, is like a miracle to confirm our faith. All that is earthly is vanity and vexation. Those who now have the most established prosperity, will soon be out of sight and forgotten.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe merchandise of Tyre.1–25Its fall and ruin.26–36
Tyre's trade and riches (verses 1–25)

People who live comfortably are still to be pitied if they are unprepared for trouble.

No one should consider themselves truly beautiful or adorned except to the extent that they have been made holy.

The description of Tyre's trade reminds us that God sees what people do while conducting ordinary business.

He watches us not only when we are at church, praying and listening, but also at markets and fairs, while buying and selling.

We should preserve a conscience free of wrongdoing in all our dealings.

As the common Father of humanity, God gives different countries different resources.

One nation produces an abundance of something another lacks, and their goods can serve the needs, comfort and even enjoyment of human life.

Trade is a blessing when conducted in reverence for God.

Besides essentials, many goods become valuable chiefly through custom. Yet God permits us to enjoy them.

But when riches increase, we easily set our hearts on them and forget the Lord who gives us the ability to gain wealth.

Tyre's downfall warns those who trust worldly power (verses 26–36)

Even the strongest and most impressive kingdoms eventually fall.

Those who make created things their ultimate confidence will fall along with what they trust.

Happy are those whose help is the God of Jacob, and whose hope rests in the Lord, who lives forever.

People engaged in trade should conduct their business according to God's word.

Those who possess wealth must remember that they are stewards of God's property and should use it to do good to everyone.

Let us seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness.

Those who engage in trade should learn to conduct their business according to God's word. Those who possess wealth should remember they are the Lord's stewards, and should use his goods in doing good to all. Let us seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe sentence against the prince or king of Tyre.1–19The fall of Zidon.20–23The restoration of Israel.24–26
The king of Tyre is humbled for pride (verses 1–19)

Henry identifies the prince or king of Tyre as Ethbaal, or Ithobal.

Lifted up by excessive pride, this ruler claimed honors belonging to God.

Pride is especially characteristic of fallen human nature.

No wisdom except that which God gives can bring lasting happiness, whether in this life or the life to come.

The proud ruler imagined that he could protect his people through his own power and regarded himself as equal to the inhabitants of heaven.

Yet even if we could live in the garden of Eden or enter heaven itself, we would find no true happiness without a humble, holy and spiritual heart.

Spiritual pride in particular comes from the devil.

Those who cherish it must expect destruction.

Sidon is judged and Israel promised restoration (verses 20–26)

The people of Sidon lived near Israel.

They could have learned to glorify the Lord.

Instead, they led Israelites into the worship of their own idols.

War and disease can be instruments of divine judgment.

But God will also reveal his glory by restoring his people to security and well-being.

He will heal them of their sins and relieve their suffering.

This promise will find its complete fulfillment in the heavenly Canaan, where all the saints are gathered, everything offensive is removed, and every grief and fear ends forever.

Blessed are God's church and all who truly belong to it, even while they are poor, afflicted or despised.

The Lord will reveal his truth, power and mercy through the salvation and happiness of his redeemed people.

Verses 1-19 Ethbaal, or Ithobal, was the prince or king of Tyre; and being lifted up with excessive pride, he claimed Divine honours. Pride is peculiarly the sin of our fallen nature. Nor can any wisdom, except that which the Lord gives, lead to happiness in this world or in that which is to come. The haughty prince of Tyre thought he was able to protect his people by his own power, and considered himself as equal to the inhabitants of heaven. If it were possible to dwell in the garden of Eden, or even to enter heaven, no solid happiness could be enjoyed without a humble, holy, and spiritual mind. Especially all spiritual pride is of the devil. Those who indulge therein must expect to perish.
[Ezek.28.20-Ezek.28.26]
Verses 20-26 . The Zidonians were borderers upon the land of Israel, and they might have learned to glorify the Lord; but, instead of that, they seduced Israel to the worship of their idols. War and pestilence are God's messengers; but he will be glorified in the restoring his people to their former safety and prosperity. God will cure them of their sins, and ease them of their troubles. This promise will at length fully come to pass in the heavenly Canaan: when all the saints shall be gathered together, every thing that offends shall be removed, all griefs and fears for ever banished. Happy, then, is the church of God, and every living member of it, though poor, afflicted, and despised; for the Lord will display his truth, power, and mercy, in the salvation and happiness of his redeemed people.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe desolation of Egypt.1–16Also a promise of mercy to Israel.17–21
Egypt's boasting and its ruin (verses 1–16)

Worldly people boast about their possessions while forgetting that everything they have came from God and ought to be used for him.

What reason do we have to boast?

Self is the great idol that people everywhere worship in disregard of God and his authority.

The Lord can drive people away from the very circumstances in which they feel most secure and comfortable.

Those who cling to such a person or source of security may perish along with it.

That is how pride, presumption and false confidence end.

God opposes those who harm his people, and even more those who lead them into sin.

Egypt would become a kingdom again, but a very lowly kingdom, with little wealth or political power.

Henry says its later history shows the fulfillment of the prophecy.

It is not only in justice, but also in wisdom and goodness toward us, that the Lord sometimes breaks the created supports on which we lean, so they will no longer be our confidence.

God recompenses Babylon and preserves mercy for Israel (verses 17–21)

Those who besieged Tyre gained little plunder.

But when God uses ambitious or greedy people for his purposes, he may reward them according to the desires of their own hearts; everyone receives an appropriate recompense.

Mercy would soon be shown to the house of Israel.

The history of nations helps explain ancient prophecies, and events fulfill God's word.

Even in the deepest trouble, the Lord can be sowing the seeds of future well-being.

Happy are those who seek his favor, grace and likeness.

They delight in serving him and do not covet an earthly reward.

The blessings they seek will remain theirs forever.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.29.1-Ezek.29.16]
Chapter 29
The desolation of Egypt. ( [Ezek.29.1-Ezek.29.16] Ezek 29:1-16) Also a promise of mercy to Israel. ( [Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21] Ezek 29:17-21)
Verses 1-16 Worldly, carnal minds pride themselves in their property, forgetting that whatever we have, we received it from God, and should use it for God. Why, then, do we boast? Self is the great idol which all the world worships, in contempt of God and his sovereignty. God can force men out of that in which they are most secure and easy. Such a one, and all that cleave to him, shall perish together. Thus end men's pride, presumption, and carnal security. The Lord is against those who do harm to his people, and still more against those who lead them into sin. Egypt shall be a kingdom again, but it shall be the basest of the kingdoms; it shall have little wealth and power. History shows the complete fulfilment of this prophecy. God, not only in justice, but in wisdom and goodness to us, breaks the creature-stays on which we lean, that they may be no more our confidence.
[Ezek.29.17-Ezek.29.21]
Verses 17-21 The besiegers of Tyre obtained little plunder. But when God employs ambitious or covetous men, he will recompense them according to the desires of their hearts; for every man shall have his reward. God had mercy in store for the house of Israel soon after. The history of nations best explains ancient prophecies. All events fulfil the Scriptures. Thus, in the deepest scenes of adversity, the Lord sows the seed of our future prosperity. Happy are those who desire his favour, grace, and image; they will delight in his service, and not covet any earthly recompence; and the blessings they have chosen shall be sure to them for ever.

This prophecy gives a full account of Egypt's coming destruction.

Those who join themselves to God's enemies will share in their punishment.

The king of Babylon and his army would become instruments of that destruction.

God often makes one wicked person a means of judgment against another.

No place in Egypt would escape the fury of the Chaldeans.

The Lord makes himself known through the judgments he executes.

Yet all these are only present effects of divine displeasure.

Egypt would become weaker and weaker.

He justly breaks power that has been abused to oppress or cheat others.

Babylon would grow stronger.

It is useless to try to bind up the arm God has decided to break, or to strengthen people he has determined to bring down.

Those who disregard the revelations of God's truth and mercy will come to know his power and justice through the punishment of their sins.
